ai.definition: AI safety refers to the development and implementation of methods and standards to ensure that artificial intelligence systems operate safely and ethically in their intended environments.
ai.howItWorks: AI safety involves creating robust ethical guidelines, developing comprehensive test frameworks, and implementing continuous monitoring mechanisms. These steps help identify potential risks and mitigate them before they can cause harm.
ai.problemSolved: The problem of ensuring that AI systems are safe for deployment and use in various applications, including autonomous vehicles, healthcare, finance, and more.
ai.manufacturing: AI safety is not directly related to the physical manufacturing process but rather focuses on the design, testing, and operation of AI systems.
ai.buildProcess: The build process involves developing ethical guidelines, creating test frameworks, and establishing monitoring protocols. This includes defining acceptable use cases, ensuring transparency in decision-making processes, and continuously evaluating system performance against these standards.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development and maintenance of ethical guidelines, testing infrastructure, and continuous monitoring systems. Additionally, there are costs associated with training developers and operators on safe AI practices.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: AI safety is expected to become increasingly important as AI technologies continue to integrate into various sectors, driving demand for more rigorous safety standards and practices.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by country but are becoming more common. Governments and industry bodies are starting to establish guidelines and frameworks to ensure the safe deployment of AI systems.
ai.risks: Potential risks include unintended consequences from AI decisions, lack of transparency in decision-making processes, and ethical violations such as bias or privacy breaches.
ai.profitability: Profitability is dependent on the successful implementation of safety measures, which can lead to increased trust and adoption of AI technologies. However, there are costs associated with these measures that must be managed.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on refining ethical guidelines, improving test frameworks, and enhancing monitoring capabilities. There may also be a push for more standardized approaches across industries.

glossary.def: A set of principles designed to ensure that AI systems operate in a manner consistent with ethical standards.
Structured approaches for evaluating and validating the safety, reliability, and performance of AI systems.
Ongoing processes to track and assess the behavior and outcomes of AI systems in real-time.

subsystems.name: Threat modelling and requirements
subsystems.role: defines what failure looks like for a given system and which failures are unacceptable.

subsystems.name: Evaluation and benchmarking
subsystems.role: measures both capability and harmful behaviour in a repeatable way.

subsystems.name: Red-teaming
subsystems.role: deliberately attacks the system to find failures before users do.

subsystems.name: Alignment training
subsystems.role: shapes model behaviour during training rather than filtering it afterwards.

subsystems.name: Interpretability and monitoring
subsystems.role: looks inside the model and watches its behaviour over time.

subsystems.name: Inference-time guardrails
subsystems.role: catches harmful inputs and outputs while the system is running.

subsystems.name: Governance and assurance
subsystems.role: makes safety claims checkable by people outside the developer.
parts: risk-management frameworks such as the NIST AI RMF
conformity assessment under the EU AI Act

buildSteps.title: Define the threat model
buildSteps.detail: For the specific deployment, list plausible misuse, accident and failure modes, and set which outcomes are unacceptable rather than merely undesirable.

buildSteps.title: Build data and feedback pipelines
buildSteps.detail: Assemble evaluation datasets and a workforce that can label harmful, helpful and borderline outputs consistently, with quality control on the annotators.

buildSteps.title: Train with an alignment objective
buildSteps.detail: Fine-tune the base model on demonstrations and preference comparisons so it refuses clearly harmful requests and explains uncertainty, then check that this did not degrade capability.

buildSteps.title: Construct the evaluation suite
buildSteps.detail: Combine public benchmarks with private held-out tests, including automated graders and human review, and freeze a version so results are comparable across model releases.

buildSteps.title: Red-team iteratively
buildSteps.detail: Expert teams and automated attack tools try jailbreaks, prompt injection and capability elicitation; every failure found is patched and re-tested until the suite is stable.

buildSteps.title: Add inference-time guardrails
buildSteps.detail: Wrap the model in input and output classifiers, restrict which tools and data it can reach, and sandbox any code execution.

buildSteps.title: Probe the internals
buildSteps.detail: Use interpretability tools to check whether the model represents and uses concepts the way its outputs suggest, rather than relying on behaviour alone.

buildSteps.title: Document and audit
buildSteps.detail: Publish or file system cards, evaluation results and residual risks; submit to external review or conformity assessment where regulation requires it.

buildSteps.title: Monitor after deployment
buildSteps.detail: Log real-world usage for new failure modes, feed incidents back into the evaluation suite, and retrain or withdraw the system when thresholds are crossed.

prerequisites.why: evaluations, red-teaming and guardrails all need repeated access to the model at production scale.
alignment training depends on large volumes of consistent human judgements, often from contract workforces.

prerequisites.tech: Interpretability methods that scale to large models
prerequisites.why: feature-level analysis works on small models and selected layers, not yet as a full audit of a frontier system.

prerequisites.tech: Evaluation for capabilities beyond human expertise
prerequisites.why: if a model can do something no human can verify, benchmarks and human graders cannot confirm whether it did it safely or correctly.
proving properties holds for small networks and narrow input ranges, and does not currently scale to frontier models.
the EU AI Act and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework provide structure, but enforcement and technical standards are still being written.

pathway.milestone: frontier developers run internal red teams, publish system cards and apply runtime filters; general-purpose AI obligations begin applying under the EU AI Act
pathway.unlocks: a baseline of documented practice and incident reporting.

pathway.milestone: standardised third-party evaluations and repeatable audits
pathway.unlocks: safety claims that buyers, regulators and insurers can compare across developers.

pathway.milestone: interpretability mature enough to check properties directly instead of sampling behaviour
pathway.unlocks: assurance that does not depend on the model failing in a test first.

pathway.milestone: scalable oversight methods for systems that outperform their overseers
pathway.unlocks: a credible path to deploying very capable systems under meaningful human control.
